results.title: Scaling Up Liquid-Resistance Liquid-Capacitance Networks for Efficient Sequence Modeling
results.content: We present LrcSSM, a \textit{nonlinear} recurrent model that processes long sequences as fast as today's linear state-space layers. By forcing the state-transition matrix to be diagonal and learned at every step, the full sequence can be solved in parallel with a single prefix-scan, giving O(T D)\mathcal{O}(TD) time and memory and only O(log⁡T)\mathcal{O}(\log T) sequential depth, for input-sequence length T and a state dimension D. Lastly, for network depth L, as the forward and backward passes cost Θ(T D L)\Theta(T\,D\,L) FLOPs, with its low sequential depth and parameter count Θ(D L)\Theta(D\,L), the model follows the compute-optimal scaling law regime (β≈0.42\beta \approx 0.42) recently observed for Mamba, outperforming quadratic-attention Transformers at equal compute while avoiding the memory overhead of FFT-based long convolutions. to a competitive NSSM on long sequences and compare it to state of the art LSSMs. We discuss in detail ho w to scale LRCs to LrcSSMs having a diagonal nonlinear state-and-. state-transition matrix of LrcSSMs to be diagonal and learned at every time step,the full sequence. Albert Gu and T ri Dao.Mamba:Linear-time sequence modeling with selective state spaces. The resulting models represent dynamical systems with varying (i.e., liquid) time-constants coupled to their hidden state, with outputs being computed by numerical differential equation solvers. A promising recent approach proposed modeling sequences by simulating the fundamental state space model (SSM) x′(t)=A x(t)+B u(t),y(t)=C x(t)+D u(t) x'(t) = Ax(t) + Bu(t), y(t) = Cx(t) + Du(t) , and showed that for appropriate choices of the state matrix A , this system could handle long-range dependencies mathematically and empirically. We propose the Structured State Space (S4) sequence model based on a new parameterization for the SSM, and show that it can be computed much more efficiently than prior approaches while preserving their theoretical strengths. S4 achieves strong empirical results across a diverse range of established benchmarks, including (i) 91\% accuracy on sequential CIFAR-10 with no data augmentation or auxiliary losses, on par with a larger 2-D ResNet, (ii) substantially closing the gap to Transformers on image and language modeling tasks, while performing generation 60×60\times faster (iii) SoTA on every task from the Long Range Arena benchmark, including solving the challenging Path-X task of length 16k that all prior work fails on, while being as efficient as all competitors.

results.title: Mamba-ND: Selective State Space Modeling for Multi-Dimensional Data
results.content:
Title: Mamba-ND: Selective State Space Modeling for Multi-Dimensional Data
Empirically, we show that Mamba-ND demonstrates performance competitive with the state-of-the-art on various multi-dimensional benchmarks, including ImageNet-1K classification, HMDB-51 and UCF-101 action recognition, ERA5 weather forecasting and BTCV 3D segmentation. A natural extension of this method, which we call ND-SSM, is to process the input in 2⁢D2𝐷2D2 italic\_D directions, where D𝐷Ditalic\_D is the dimension of the data, and aggregate the results. Mamba-ND does not introduce any complicated changes to 1D-SSM layers. By stacking 1D-SSM layers as black boxes and alternating the sequence order between each layer, Mamba-ND was able to surpass Transformer-based models on various tasks, including image classification, action recognition, and weather forecasting and 3D segmentation, with a lower parameter count. In this work, we discuss various alternative ways to extend SSM to higher dimensions by flattening the input data into 1D sequences. As mentioned in Sec. 3.2, a Mamba layer consists of a 1D convolution, an SSM kernel, and a residual connection. To provide a concrete example, the ordering (W⁢H)−limit-from𝑊𝐻(WH)-( italic\_W italic\_H ) - refers to first permuting the 2D data into a 2D array of W×H𝑊𝐻W\times Hitalic\_W × italic\_H, then flattening it into a 1D sequence in row-major order, and finally reversing the order of this 1D sequence. After extensive experiments, our final design uses the standard 1D-SSM layer and an alternating-directional: (H+H-W+W-T+T-) at the block level. This sequence is then passed through K𝐾Kitalic\_K Mamba-ND blocks, each of which consists of a chain of 1-D SSM layers that process the sequence in alternating orderings. Since we adopted an alternating design, each layer only sees a 1D input sequence. Compared with the 1D-Mamba baseline, in which no special design is adopted after naively flattening the multi-dimensional sequence into a 1D sequence, we achieved a +4.84.8+4.8+ 4.8 accuracy on ImageNet and a +26.926.9+26.9+ 26.9 accuracy on HMDB-51. In addition to three choices discussed in Sec. 4.3, we also experiment with a hex-directional design [H+H-W+W-T+T-], in which inputs of a block are processed by multiple layers at different ordering in parallel, and the results are summed together in the end. For ERA5 weather forecast, we use a 12 layer version of Mamba-3D-B.

results.content:
Title: java - Creating a Graph Query Language (Node/Edge/HyperEdge) - Stack Overflow
### more stack exchange communities. # Creating a Graph Query Language (Node/Edge/HyperEdge). `Node1(w/ attributes) -- > Edge1(w/ attr.) -- > Node2(w/ attr.)`. What I have so far, is a visitor pattern set up to traverse the Nodes/Edges/HyperEdges, and this allows for a sort of querying, but it's not very simple, since you have to create a new visitor for new types of queries. The code above, does a query that checks if the starting node has a mass of `2.5` and a linked node (child) has no attributes. The visitor does a `condition.check( Node )` and returns a boolean. Personally, I like the idea of the visitor pattern, however it might turn out to expensive to visit all nodes. I would separate the code for "moving on the graph" (like "check whether visited node fulfills condition" or "check whether connected nodes fulfill condition") from the code that actually checks (or is) a condition. `// Select nodes with mass 2.5, follow edges with both conditions fulfilled and check that the children on these edges have no attributes. (I used "freestyle" because of missing creativity right now, but the intention of it should be clear) Node that in general this might be two different interfaces in order to not build strange queries. The `QuerySelector` implementations would than be responsible for "moving" around the visited nodes whereas the `Conditition` implementation would check whether the condition match. One idea which is popping up is to add (for each index) a layer to the graph in which each nodes models one of the different attribute settings for the "indexed variable". The normal edges could then connect these index nodes with the nodes in the original graph. If you have some kind of Index make sure that the index can as well receive a visitor such that it does not have to visit all nodes in the graph. You can create any kind of linear query pattern using this style; and if you add a some extra state you could even do branching queries by e.g. setName("A") and later .node("A") to return to that point of the query.
